programme.title: Yes, Minister
programme.desc: Jim Hacker finds himself in the middle of a major row over the British Chemical Corporation, and Sir Humphrey tries to get Jim to support the politically unpopular measure.

programme.title: Plague Fiction
programme.desc: Professor Laura Ashe takes a look back at the Black Death of the 14th century, the deadliest pandemic in human history. Going from one of the earliest accounts of plague in 1347 through to Samuel Pepys's record of the Great Plague of London in the 1660s, Professor Ashe explores how literature helped us cope with fear and tragedy, the importance of bravery and personal sacrifice, and whether the words of the past can offer us the comfort and healing that we need now.

programme.title: Agatha Christie: Lucy Worsley on the Mystery Queen
programme.desc: Historian Lucy Worsley investigates the complex factors that shaped the dark imagination of a refined Devonshire lady, discovering family secrets and a childhood haunted by a sinister figure.

programme.title: Britain's Most Fragile Treasure
programme.desc: Historian Dr Janina Ramirez unlocks the secrets of a centuries-old masterpiece in glass, the East Window at York Minster - the largest medieval stained-glass window in the country and the creative vision of a master craftsman called John Thornton. Within its 311 panels is the entire history of the world.

programme.title: BBC Proms
programme.sub-title: 2025: Ravel's Piano Concerto for the Left Hand
programme.desc: Nicholas McCarthy, the world's only professional one-handed concert pianist, makes his Proms debut alongside the Bournemouth Symphony Orchestra in a concert of 20th-century classics.

programme.title: A Voice for the World: Stuart Burrows
programme.desc: A profile from 1977 of Welsh tenor Stuart Burrows, who achieved international acclaim in the opera houses and concert halls of the world. Burrows is seen at home in Wales and at work in London, Paris and New York. He is shown in rehearsal and in performance, and the programme includes arias from Eugene Onegin, Don Giovanni and Manon, together with a few well-loved ballads and a favourite Welsh folk song. There are also tributes from Sir Georg Solti and Beverly Sills.

programme.title: Stuart Burrows Sings
programme.desc: Celebrated Welsh tenor Stuart Burrows is joined at St David's Hall, Cardiff, by soprano Karita Mattila, a young Aled Jones, the Pendyrus Male Choir, and soprano Beverley Humphreys.

programme.title: A Concerto for Evelyn
programme.desc: From the 1992 BBC Proms, the premiere of James MacMillan's concerto for percussion and orchestra, Veni, Veni, Emmanuel, composed for Evelyn Glennie. Jukka-Pekka Saraste conducts the Scottish Chamber Orchestra.

programme.title: This Cultural Life
programme.desc: The world's leading classical solo percussionist Evelyn Glennie talks to John Wilson about her career and some of the key influences on her artistic path. From growing up in rural Aberdeenshire and becoming profoundly deaf at a young age, Glennie traces her route to fulfilling the ambition of becoming the first full-time solo percussionist.

programme.title: Maurice Ravel
programme.desc: Documentary about French composer Maurice Ravel (1875-1937), narrated by John Abineri and featuring performances of his work by Jill Gomez, Osian Ellis, Edward Beckett and others.

programme.sub-title: The Severn: From Docks to Rocks
programme.desc: Angela Rippon visits Bristol's historic harbour on the day of the maritime carnival and takes a pleasure cruise through the Avon Gorge and back to the Severn Estuary.

programme.title: The Flying Archaeologist
programme.desc: Archaeologist Ben Robinson flies over Wiltshire to uncover sites discovered through aerial phototographs. These have led to new evidence about Stonehenge that explains the reason for its location and how long ago it was occupied.

programme.title: Singapore 1942: End of Empire
programme.desc: A 70th-anniversary television event telling the story of how the fall of Singapore in 1942 shattered myths, brought an empire to its knees, and changed the destiny of millions of people. This episode looks at how Japan's lightning invasion of Malaya threatened the key British port of Singapore, igniting ethnic and political tensions, and tells how Scottish soldiers were at the heart of the city's defence.

programme.title: Rise of the Nazis
programme.desc: In April 1945, the Nazis organise one of the final acts of the Third Reich, a concert by the Berlin Philharmonic, including the last scene of the opera Die Gotterdammerung, which features a suicide at its centre. It's a clear sign that Hitler and many of his supporters are going to end it all.

programme.title: Hiroshima
programme.desc: The development of the atomic bomb and the decision to use it against Japan.

programme.title: Berlin 1945
programme.desc: The British, French and Americans are waiting to enter Berlin. In the meantime, the Soviets appoint mayors, organise the food supply and go on the hunt for war criminals. The Jewish community, among whom there are few survivors, regroup.

programme.title: Ocean Autopsy: The Secret Story of Our Seas
programme.desc: Two-thirds of the planet is covered in water, split into five distinct oceans but part of one huge global water system, a system that has been shaping human destiny for millions of years. Now, it is mankind that is shaping the destiny of the oceans.

programme.title: The Flying Archaeologist
programme.desc: Archaeologist Ben Robinson flies over the Broads where aerial photos have discovered a staggering 945 previously unknown ancient sites, many of which have historians rethinking the history of the area. Archaeologists have now discovered a key piece of evidence to unravel why the Roman town of Caistor St Edmund never became a modern town, along with proof of a Bronze Age settlement near Ormseby.

programme.title: The Good Life
programme.desc: Barbara and Tom find it almost impossible to catch the early worm as their early rising disturbs their neighbours the Leadbetters.

programme.title: Yes, Minister
programme.desc: Jim Hacker is upset by rumours of a cabinet reshuffle and decides to take drastic action to keep his post.

programme.title: The First Georgians: The German Kings who Made Britain
programme.desc: Dr Lucy Worsley's story of the first Georgian kings reaches the final years of George II's reign. With extensive access to artworks in the Royal Collection, she shows how Britain's new ruling family fought the French, the Jacobites and each other, all at the same time. However, while George very publicly bickered with his troublesome son Frederick, Prince of Wales, he also led from the front on the battlefield, and helped turn his adopted nation into a global superpower.

programme.title: The Death of Yugoslavia
programme.sub-title: Eyewitness to History: The Death of Yugoslavia - Part 2
programme.desc: Norma Percy and Paul Mitchell look back on the documentary series `The Death of Yugoslavia'.

programme.title: The Death of Yugoslavia
programme.desc: Croatia recaptures most of the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Bosnian Serb forces commit massacres. NATO forces the Bosnian Serbs to return to negotiations. The Dayton Agreement effectively ends the Bosnian war.

programme.title: Imagine...
programme.desc: Alan Yentob chronicles the life and work of 2014's Man Booker Prize winner Richard Flanagan. Alan journeys with Flanagan through his native Tasmania and on to Thailand, to see first-hand the site of the `Death Railway'.

programme.title: Storyville
programme.desc: For director Roger Ross Williams, prison was not a distant possibility when he was growing up, but a daily threat. `As a young black man in a chaotic environment, I always felt there was a chance that, whether or not I committed a crime, I could end up behind bars.' Determined to avoid this fate, Roger left his hometown of Easton, Pennsylvania as a teenager to pursue his dreams of being a film-maker.

programme.title: Dame Maggie Smith - A Celebration
programme.desc: A special tribute to the celebrated and enigmatic actress Dame Maggie Smith, who remains a mystery to her friends and perhaps also to herself - hear the story of her remarkable life told by those who knew her best as they celebrate her much-loved appearances across film and TV spanning almost 70 years. Maggie, who passed away in September 2024, is beloved the world over for her countless iconic screen performances - in recent years she gained a new level of popularity playing the razor-tongued Lady Violet Crawley in Downton Abbey, but Maggie remained a very private person who had little time for the trappings that came with fame in spite of her success. Using Maggie's own voice as its heartbeat - and featuring personal accounts from close friends and colleagues from across her career - the film tells the story of a girl born in pre-war Essex who took Broadway and the West End by storm against the odds before eventually becoming one of the nation's most popular and respected performers.
